objective_for_doctor: Assess and diagnose the patient presenting with progressive left leg pain.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Doctor: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today? Patient: I’ve had progressive pain in my left leg for about two months, and it’s gotten bad enough to interfere with my sleep. It started after I got hit on that leg with a baseball—there was redness and swelling afterward—and ibuprofen hasn’t helped.
Doctor: Can you describe exactly where on your left leg the pain is located and what it feels like (e.g., sharp, aching, throbbing, burning)?

Patient: The pain is mostly in the lower part of my left leg, around the shin/ankle area, and it feels deep and achy but sometimes throbs. It seems to be getting worse over time and hurts even when I’m resting.
Doctor: Since the injury, have you noticed any swelling, redness, warmth, or visible bruising on that leg, either continuously or intermittently?

Patient: Yes—there was clear redness and swelling right after the baseball hit, and the area still looks a bit warmer at times. I haven’t noticed any bruising spreading, but the swelling and redness come and go while the pain keeps getting worse.
Doctor: Have you had any fever, chills, night sweats, or feeling generally unwell since the injury began?
Patient: No fever, chills, or night sweats, and I haven’t felt sick otherwise. I just have the worsening left leg pain, which is now bad enough to wake me and keep me from sleeping.

Doctor: Have you noticed any changes in skin color, temperature (hot or cold compared to the other leg), swelling that’s out of proportion, or increased sensitivity to touch (pain from light pressure) in the affected area?

Patient: The skin over the area sometimes looks more reddish and feels warmer than my other leg, and it’s more tender to touch than before—light pressure can make it hurt. The swelling doesn’t seem huge all the time, but it’s been coming and going along with the warmth.
Doctor: Have you had any difficulty walking or bearing weight on that leg, or does the pain worsen when you try to move the ankle or foot?

Patient: Walking is hard now—I limp and I try to avoid putting full weight on my left leg. When I move my ankle or foot, the pain tends to get worse, even though I don’t really feel a specific joint click or anything.

Doctor: When a clinician gently moves (passively stretches) the muscles around your shin—like dorsiflexing your foot—does that make the pain markedly worse, or does the area feel unusually tight or firm?

Patient: Yes, when my foot is gently moved up toward my shin, the pain definitely gets worse, and the area feels tight and tender, like it’s pulling. It’s not just the ankle joint—it seems deeper in the lower leg muscles.

Doctor: Have you noticed any changes in sensation over the affected area—such as increased sensitivity to light touch (allodynia), tingling, numbness, or a burning feeling that’s different from the deep ache?

Patient: I haven’t had any numbness or tingling, but the skin in that spot feels more sensitive than before—light touch can really trigger the pain. It’s mostly a deep achy pain with occasional throbbing, not a burning feeling.
Doctor: After the baseball hit, did the skin on your shin ever break open, develop a cut, ulcer, or any drainage/pus that you’ve noticed?
Patient: No, the skin didn’t break open and I haven’t seen any drainage or pus. The redness and swelling were there after the hit, but it didn’t turn into an open wound.
Doctor: Have you noticed any changes in the skin of that leg—such as increased sweating, shiny or thin skin, loss or excess of hair, or nail changes—compared with the other leg?

Patient: I haven’t noticed any unusual sweating, shiny or thin-looking skin, or changes in hair, and my nails look the same as the other leg. The main difference is that the same area sometimes looks more reddish and feels warmer and more tender.
Doctor: Does the pain get noticeably better or worse with activity—such as walking, standing, or exercising—or with elevation of the leg?

Patient: The pain gets worse when I walk or stand, so I’m limping to avoid putting weight on it, but it also hurts when I’m resting. I haven’t tried elevating it enough to say it clearly helps, though lying still doesn’t make it go away.
Doctor: On examination, does the area feel firm or “rock‑hard” when I press on the shin, suggesting a tight compartment or a hard mass, or is it more soft and fluctuant?

Doctor: On examination, does the area feel firm or “rock‑hard” when I press on the shin, suggesting a tight compartment or a hard mass, or is it more soft and fluctuant? Patient: When I press, it feels firm and tight rather than squishy, and it’s very tender—especially when the foot is gently moved. I don’t feel any clear soft pocket or fluctuation.
Doctor: Do you have any chronic medical conditions such as diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, immune‑system disorders, or are you taking medications that suppress immunity?

Doctor: Do you have any chronic medical conditions such as diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, immune‑system disorders, or are you taking medications that suppress immunity? Patient: No, I don’t have any chronic conditions and I’m not on any medicines that suppress my immune system. I’ve only tried ibuprofen, but it hasn’t helped my leg pain.
Doctor: When you run your fingers over the painful area, do you feel a distinct hard lump or mass that seems to be getting larger, or is the tissue just uniformly firm without a defined nodule?

Patient: I don’t feel a single distinct lump, but the tissue in that spot feels uniformly tight and firm and it seems to be getting worse over time. It’s very tender when I press there, especially when my foot is moved upward toward my shin.
